Still
STIL
adj. / adv. / v.
Webster 1828 prints STILL as verb (to stop motion or noise; to calm), adjective (silent, quiet, motionless), noun (calm; also the distilling vessel), and adverb (to this time; nevertheless; always). This page keeps two longer senses in one spelling: quiet that stops, and 'yet / to this time.' The distilling vessel is a third spelling-share; it is not mashed into the biblical quiet. Companion pages already treat rest, wait, and peace.

Biblical Definition

Still is one spelling with two honest senses. Do not mash them.

1. Quiet, stopped, not agitated. To still is to check motion or noise. To be still is to be silent, calm, motionless. Moses says to the people, Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD. The psalm says, Be still, and know that I am God. This is not emptied mind. It is stopped panic under a God who will be exalted in the earth.

2. Yet; to this time; nevertheless. The adverb keeps a fact in force: it is still true; he is still afraid; they kept still the office. Scripture's quiet is not the same word as 'still going.' The dictionary therefore keeps still from becoming a spa verb. God stills, or you are only holding your breath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828: STILL, verb — to stop motion or noise; to calm. STILL, adjective — silent; quiet; motionless. STILL, adverb — to this time; nevertheless; always. A separate noun names the distilling vessel.

expand to see more

STILL, verb transitive

1. To stop, as motion or agitation; to check or restrain; to make quiet; as, to still the raging sea.

2. To stop, as noise; to silence.

3. To appease; to calm; to quiet; as tumult, agitation or excitement; as, to still the passions.

STILL, adjective

1. Silent; uttering no sound.

3. Motionless; as, to stand still; to lie or sit still.

STILL, adverb

1. To this time; till now.

2. Nevertheless; notwithstanding.

STILL, noun [Latin , to drop. See Distill.] A vessel, boiler or copper used in the distillation of liquors.

Key Scripture

Psalm 46:10 — "Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!"

Exodus 14:13 — "And Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which He will accomplish for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall see again no more forever."

Modern Corruption

Still is corrupted when 'be still' is recast as emptied-mind wellness, when standing still is mocked as passivity, and when the adverb 'still' is used to keep a sin in force as if time had baptized it.

expand to see more

The first corruption is mindfulness as Scripture. Psalm 46:10 is Be still, and know that I am God — not be still and know yourself. The age sells stillness as a nervous-system hack. The psalm sells the knowledge of God and His exaltation among the nations.

The second corruption is motion as virtue. Exodus 14:13 is Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD. Hustle calls that weakness. Israel would have died in the water they tried to manage.

The third corruption is the adverb as excuse. 'We still do it this way' can be fidelity, or it can be unbelief with a calendar. Webster's nevertheless does not pardon what God has named sin.

Usage

"Be still, and know that I am God — knowledge, not vacancy (Psalm 46:10)."

"Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD (Exodus 14:13)."

"Keep the quiet sense and the 'yet' sense apart; do not baptize a still with gin."
